lessons.title: Lesson 1: Your transferable skills
lessons.text:
Lesson 1 of 6 · about 5 minutes
Goal: Name five skills from sport that transfer to work, each with a real example.
This lesson builds toward: Given your roles, routines and challenges in sport, you will list five transferable skills with a real sports example for each, with every example true and specific enough to count as proof.
Transferable skills are skills you can use in many jobs. Sport builds lots of them: teamwork, leadership, time management, handling pressure, taking feedback, discipline, communication and resilience after losses.
Employers want proof, not just words. "Leadership" is a claim. "Captain of a 20-player team; ran warm-ups and settled conflicts" is proof.
An AI assistant can help you find skills you did not notice: "I've played four years of varsity soccer, was captain senior year, balanced practice with a part-time job, and came back from an ACL injury. What transferable skills does this show, with one example each?" Keep only what is true.
Step by step:
- List what you did in sport: roles, routines, challenges.
- Ask AI which skills they show.
- Pick five skills.
- Write a real example for each.
- Remove anything that is not true.
Words to know:
- Transferable skill: a skill you can use in many different jobs.
- Resilience: bouncing back after a setback.
Try it now: Use an AI assistant to find skills in your sports experience. Write your top five, each with a true example.
You can now name your transferable skills and prove each with an example.

check.why: Transferable skills, like taking feedback, can be used in many jobs.

check.q: You wrote "teamwork" on your list. How do you make it proof?
options: Add a real example, like organizing team study sessions before away games
Ask AI to make it sound bigger
check.why: Employers want proof, so add a real example.

lessons.title: Lesson 2: Your 60-second athlete story
lessons.text:
Lesson 2 of 6 · about 5 minutes
Goal: Write and practice a 60-second story about who you are and where you are going.
This lesson builds toward: Using the Past, Present and Future structure, you will write and say a 60-second story about who you are and where you are going, about 150 words, in your own voice, and practiced out loud until it sounds natural.
People will ask "Tell me about yourself" in interviews, networking and even recruiting. Have a 60-second answer ready.
Use three parts: Past (sport and what it taught you), Present (what you are doing now: school, work, training), Future (the direction you are curious about). Example: "I've played basketball for ten years, and being captain taught me how to lead a group under pressure. Now I'm studying business and working part-time at a gym. I'm interested in sports marketing and want to learn how teams build fan communities."
Ask an AI assistant to tighten it to about 150 words, then practice it out loud until it sounds natural, not memorized.
Step by step:
- Write your Past, Present and Future in a sentence or two each.
- Ask AI to tighten it to about 150 words.
- Edit it into your voice.
- Practice out loud three times.
- Time yourself: about 60 seconds.
Words to know:
- Elevator pitch: a short spoken introduction you could give in an elevator ride.
- Networking: building relationships with people who can share advice and opportunities.
Try it now: Write your Past-Present-Future story, tighten it with AI, and record yourself saying it on your phone. Listen back once and fix one thing.
You can now tell your 60-second athlete story clearly and naturally.

check.q: What does the "Present" part of your story say?
options: What you are doing now: school, work, training
check.why: Past is sport, Present is what you do now, Future is your direction.

check.q: Your story sounds stiff and memorized. What do you do?
options: Practice it out loud until it sounds natural
check.why: Practice out loud until it sounds natural, not memorized.

lessons.title: Lesson 3: Life after sport: exploring careers
lessons.text:
Lesson 3 of 6 · about 5 minutes
Goal: List three careers to explore and one way to learn about each.
This lesson builds toward: Given your interests and an AI assistant, you will list three careers to explore and one way to learn about each, with education and pay checked on an official career site or with a career counselor.
Every athlete stops competing one day, by choice, injury or age. Planning early makes that change easier and gives you confidence now.
Explore careers connected to your interests, not just sport. Inside sport: coaching, athletic training, sports marketing, broadcasting, analytics, facility management. Outside sport: business, health, tech, trades, teaching, public service and more.
Use an AI assistant to brainstorm and explain careers, then check real details like education needed and pay on official career sites, such as the US Bureau of Labor Statistics' Occupational Outlook Handbook, or with a school career counselor.
Step by step:
- List your interests outside winning.
- Ask AI for careers that match.
- Pick three to explore.
- Check each on an official career site or with a career counselor.
- Write one way to learn more about each.
Words to know:
- Career counselor: a person at school or in the community who helps you explore jobs.
- Occupational Outlook Handbook: a US government guide to jobs, education needed and pay.
Official sources:
- US Bureau of Labor Statistics: Occupational Outlook Handbook
Try it now: Ask an AI assistant for ten careers that fit your interests. Pick three and look up each one's education needs on an official career site or ask your career counselor.
You can now explore careers beyond playing and check details with official sources.

check.q: Which is a career outside sport?
check.why: Teaching is outside sport; the others are careers inside sport.

check.q: AI tells you the pay for a career you like. What do you do next?
options: Check it on an official career site or with a career counselor
check.why: Check real details like pay and education on official sources.

lessons.title: Lesson 4: Building a résumé with AI
lessons.text:
Lesson 4 of 6 · about 6 minutes
Goal: Build a one-page résumé that turns sports into work language.
This lesson builds toward: Using your notes and an AI assistant, you will create a one-page résumé that describes sport in work language, with action-word bullets, numbers where true, every fact checked, no private numbers shared and a human review.
A résumé is a one-page summary of your education, experience and skills. Athletes should include sport as experience, written in work language.
Sections: Contact (name, city, professional email, phone), Education, Experience (jobs, internships, volunteering and athletics), Skills, and Honors. Write bullets that start with action words and include numbers: "Balanced 20 hours a week of training with a 3.4 GPA".
Ask an AI assistant: "Turn these notes into a one-page résumé for a sports marketing internship. Use action words and numbers." Do not paste private numbers like your Social Security number. Check every detail, and have a teacher, coach or career counselor review it.
Step by step:
- Gather your education, jobs, volunteering and sports roles.
- Ask AI for a one-page résumé draft.
- Check every fact and number.
- Use action words and numbers.
- Have a counselor, teacher or coach review it.
Words to know:
- Résumé: a one-page summary of your education, experience and skills.
- Action word: a strong verb that starts a bullet, like led, organized or trained.
Try it now: Use AI to turn your notes into a one-page résumé. Fix any wrong facts and ask one adult to review it.
You can now build a one-page résumé that shows your athlete experience in work language.

check.q: Which section of a résumé includes your phone number and professional email?
check.why: Contact has your name, city, professional email and phone.

check.q: Your AI résumé draft is ready. What do you do before sending it?
options: Check every fact and have a counselor, teacher or coach review it
check.why: Check every detail and get a human review.

lessons.title: Lesson 5: Your LinkedIn profile
lessons.text:
Lesson 5 of 6 · about 5 minutes
Goal: Set up a professional LinkedIn profile (or a career portfolio page if you are not old enough).
This lesson builds toward: If you meet LinkedIn's age rules, or using Google Sites if not, you will set up a professional profile with a photo, headline, About section, experience and skills, consistent with your résumé and with five connections made using a short personal note.
LinkedIn is a professional social network where employers, recruiters and alumni connect. Check LinkedIn's current minimum age rules before signing up; if you are too young, make a simple career page in Google Sites instead.
A strong profile has: a clear, professional photo; a headline that says who you are and where you're going ("Student-athlete | Business major | Interested in sports marketing"); an About section adapted from your 60-second story; experience including athletics; and skills.
Keep it professional and consistent with your résumé. Connect with coaches, teachers, teammates, alumni of your school and people in careers you like, with a short personal note.
Step by step:
- Check LinkedIn's current age rules.
- Add a professional photo and headline.
- Adapt your 60-second story for About.
- Add experience, including athletics.
- Connect with five people with a short note.
Words to know:
- LinkedIn: a professional social network for careers and jobs.
- Headline: the short line under your name on LinkedIn.
- Alumni: people who graduated from your school.
Try it now: Set up or update your LinkedIn profile (or a Google Sites career page if you're too young). Ask AI for three headline options and pick one.
You can now set up a professional online profile that matches your résumé.

check.q: What should a LinkedIn headline say?
options: Who you are and where you are going
check.why: A strong headline says who you are and where you are going.

check.q: You want to connect with an alum who works in sports marketing. What do you do?
options: Send a request with no message
Send a short personal note with the request
Ask them for a job right away
check.why: Connect with a short personal note.

lessons.title: Lesson 6: Networking and informational interviews
lessons.text:
Lesson 6 of 6 · about 5 minutes
Goal: Write and send a polite informational interview request.
This lesson builds toward: Given one person in a career you are curious about, you will write and send a polite informational interview request, with who you are, how you found them, why their career interests you, a small ask, three prepared questions and a thank-you after.
An informational interview is a short conversation, often 15 to 20 minutes, where you ask someone about their career. You are asking for advice, not a job.
Athletes have a great network: former teammates, alumni athletes, coaches' contacts and local business owners who support your team. Many like helping student-athletes.
Write a short request: who you are, how you found them, why their career interests you, and a clear, small ask ("Could I ask you a few questions for 15 minutes in the next few weeks?"). Prepare three questions, be on time, and send a thank-you message after.
Step by step:
- Pick one person in a career you are curious about.
- Use AI to draft a short request.
- Make it personal and polite.
- Prepare three questions.
- Send a thank-you after the talk.
Words to know:
- Informational interview: a short talk to learn about someone's career, not to ask for a job.
- Network: the people you know who can share advice and opportunities.
Try it now: Final task: finish your skills list, 60-second story, résumé and online profile, then send one informational interview request to a real person and prepare three questions.
You can now ask for and prepare an informational interview to grow your network.
How your final task is checked:
What we look at Not yet Meets Exceeds Transferable skills Fewer than five skills, or skills with no real example. Five skills, each with a true, specific sports example. Each example includes a number or result, such as team size or hours balanced. 60-second story Missing Past, Present or Future, or much longer than a minute. About 60 seconds with Past, Present and Future, in the athlete's own voice. Delivered out loud naturally and adapted for the LinkedIn About section. Résumé Over one page, untrue details, or sport left out. One page, with sport in work language, action-word bullets, checked facts and a human review. Tailored to one career or internship from the athlete's explored list. Profile No profile, or it does not match the résumé. A LinkedIn profile or career page with photo, headline, About, experience and skills, matching the résumé. Five connections made with personal notes, including alumni. Informational interview request No request sent, or it asks for a job. A polite request sent to a real person with who, how found, why and a small ask, plus three questions ready. The talk happened and a thank-you message was sent. To pass: Meets or Exceeds on every row. If a row is Not yet, fix that part and try again.

check.q: What are you asking for in an informational interview?
check.why: You ask for advice, not a job.

check.q: An alum agreed to talk for 15 minutes next week. How do you prepare?
options: Prepare three questions and be on time
Plan to talk about yourself the whole time
Bring your résumé and ask for a job
check.why: Prepare three questions, be on time and send a thank-you after.
